narrative:
The model determined that you have a 94% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your academic performance in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year academic performance. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year grades placed you in the second decile, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This was the single most influential piece of information and pulled the outcome sharply toward failure. Your LSAT score of 28 was also well below the average of 37 among accepted students, adding further weight toward a negative prediction. Finally, your first-year grades, again in the second decile compared with an average around the sixth, reinforced the same direction.

Although your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 is close to the accepted average of 3.23, your middle-income background, full-time study plans, gender, and Asian background played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance if you retake any courses, consider retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s, and then reapply. Demonstrating clear upward progress in your grades will be the most powerful way to shift future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
